sweep_summary: Burmese (nucl1310) is in the catalog as 'tonal' on Okell 1969. Three title hits: (1) Ozerov 2020 (LTBA, DOI 10.1075/ltba.20009.oze) is closed access (Unpaywall closed; GBP 15 at jbe-platform); its abstract describes phrase-level intonational accent placed by information structure in 'this tonal language' — prosody, not word stress; medium priority to acquire. (2) Green 1995 (Cornell WPCPL 10, ROA-115) downloaded open from roa.rutgers.edu and read; its 2005 revision (PL 570, DOI 10.15144/PL-570.1) downloaded open from the ANU repository (CC BY-SA) and from ROA-551: Burmese foot = one tone-bearing major syllable, minor schwa syllables unfooted and never word-final, 'tone-bearing syllables fill the role of stressed syllables' (ROA-115 p. 13) — refines, does not contradict, the tonal coding. (3) Than Than Win 2003 (SEALS VII, pp. 225-241) downloaded from the SEALang SALA archive (image-only; scanned sequentially at 300 dpi): about Burmese-accented English, with one aside that Burmese syllables receive equal stress (p. 231) — confirms no differential word stress. Also re-read Watkins 2001 JIPA (already held by the project): 'Stress is subordinate to tone in Burmese' (p. 293). No source found that supersedes Okell 1969; Green 1995/2005 is the best new first-hand statement.

new_statements.reading: Burmese has no word-stress system independent of tone. Prominence belongs to tone-bearing major (heavy) syllables, each of which is its own foot; toneless schwa minor syllables are unfooted and never word-final, so a word's final syllable is always a tone-bearing major syllable. Because (L L) feet do not exist, the foot's headedness (trochaic vs iambic) cannot be determined from stress placement (Green 2005 later calls it left-headed on mora-internal grounds). This agrees with Watkins 2001 p. 293 ('Stress is subordinate to tone in Burmese') and with the catalog's 'tonal' coding; it refines it by giving the foot/word-shape account of which syllables are prominent (major, tone-bearing) and which are reduced (schwa minor syllables).

sources.citation: Green, Antony. 1995. The prosodic structure of Burmese: a constraint-based approach. Working Papers of the Cornell Phonetics Laboratory 10: 67-96. (ROA-115 preprint)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: there is good reason to suppose that the foot in Burmese is not an iamb—either (L 'H) or ('H)—but rather a single heavy syllable ('H) only. In this case, light syllables in [L H], [L L H], and [H L H] words would remain unfooted [p. 11] ... (In Burmese and Thai—discussed below—tone-bearing syllables fill the role of stressed syllables.) As mentioned in the discussion of major and minor syllables above, Burmese allows words of the shape [L «H] and [«H], but not [L «L]. [p. 13]
sources.note: First-hand theoretical analysis: Burmese has no stress system separate from tone; the tone-bearing major (heavy) syllable is the foot and plays the role of the stressed syllable, while minor schwa syllables are unfooted (NON-FOOT(schwa)) and every word must end in a major syllable (ALIGN-R). Whether the (H) foot is trochaic or iambic is undecidable because (L L) feet do not exist (p. 13). Polysyllabic words of several major syllables are several feet/prosodic words, i.e. no single culminative word stress is posited.

sources.quote: we may assume that heavy (μμ) syllables are in fact feet; because long vowels, falling diphthongs, and vowel + consonant sequences all have more prominence on the first mora than the second, these feet may be considered left-headed and therefore trochaic. ... Any minor syllables preceding a major syllable remain unfooted [p. 13] ... The characteristics of a minor syllable in Burmese are: (i) it may only contain the vowel ə; (ii) it is an open syllable; (iii) it does not bear tone; (iv) it has only a simple (C) onset; (v) it is not the final syllable of the word. [pp. 3-4]
sources.locator: pp. 3-4 (§1, major vs minor syllables) and p. 13 (§2.3 Monosyllabic feet)
sources.note: Same analysis as Green 1995, now with the foot called a left-headed (trochaic) single heavy syllable; prominence is a property of tone-bearing major syllables, minor syllables are toneless, unfooted and never word-final. No independent word-stress rule; 'stress' appears only in the constraint NON-HEAD(schwa) (p. 20) and in references.

sources.quote: 'Burmese syllables which are not reduced have one of four tones ... Reduced syllables, the product of juncture processes (see Sprigg 1957), are unstressed and tonally non-contrastive, and may contain only the vowel /@/ ... Stress: Stress is subordinate to tone in Burmese, though it seems that function words are less stressed than non-function words.' p. 294: 'vowel quality, tone and stress are closely and inextricably connected in Burmese.'

sources.citation: Judson, Adoniram (1842). Grammatical Notices of the Burmese Language. Maulmain: American Baptist Mission Press. 91 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Judson's 'accents' are the creaky and heavy tone marks of the script, so the section is a (pre-modern) statement that Burmese syllables carry tones; it is consistent with the catalog's tonal coding and with Green/Watkins (prominence and tone-bearing syllables) but makes no statement about stress placement or the stress-tone relation, hence 'silent' on stress. Describes the literary language as known to Judson at Maulmain (manuscript of c. 1816, printed 1842).

sources.quote: This study of read-aloud stories in colloquial Burmese shows that this tonal language does resort to this sort of intonational means for information-structuring reasons. The prosody of Burmese exhibits identifiable intonational patterns, which function on the level of accentual phrases. ... Accentual phrases are organised around a single accent, the location of which depends on information structural factors.
sources.locator: abstract (jbe-platform landing page; Semantic Scholar record)
sources.note: Abstract only: treats Burmese as a tonal language whose 'accent' is an intonational, phrase-level prominence placed by information structure (one accent per accentual phrase), not a lexical word stress. Nothing on fixed word-stress placement. Unpaywall: is_oa=false, oa_status=closed; publisher sells the article (GBP 15).
